core.text: Every Latin noun changes its ending to show its job in the sentence. Naming who or what the sentence is about — the doer, or the thing being described — is the job of **the nominative (the plain naming form)**, *cāsus nōminātīvus*. It is the form the dictionary gives: *puella* (girl), *servus* (slave), *oppidum* (town). Latin does not rely on word order: the subject may come first, last or in the middle, and the ending marks it.
The subject is the person or thing the sentence is about, usually before the verb: *the girl* sings. A word after *is* that renames the subject (*Julia is a girl*) belongs with it.
The subject, and any word that renames it after *est* / *sunt* (is / are), stands in the nominative: singular -a, -us, -um; plural -ae, -ī, -a.

invented.en: The girl sings, the boy laughs.
The slaves are working in the garden.

core.text: *Mārcus Iūliam pulsat* and *Iūlia Mārcum pulsat* use the same two names, but the endings, not the order, say who hits whom. The doer keeps the naming form (*Mārcus*, *Iūlia*); the one it is done to takes -m, the accusative (the object form). A word ending in -m is not the subject.

teach.title: What the naming form does
teach.say: A Latin noun changes its tail to show its job in the sentence. Naming who or what the sentence is about — the subject — is the job of the nominative (the plain naming form). In *Nīlus fluvius magnus in Āfricā est* the sentence is about *Nīlus*, so *Nīlus* wears that form. English keeps the subject in its place in front of the verb; Latin lets it stand anywhere and marks it with the ending instead.

teach.title: a-nouns: -a for one, -ae for several
teach.say: A noun whose dictionary form ends in -a, like *īnsula* (island), keeps -a for one and changes to -ae for more than one: *īnsula* is one island, *īnsulae* is islands. Nothing else about the word moves; only the tail.

teach.title: us-nouns: -us for one, -ī for several
teach.say: *Fluvius* (river) ends in -us for one. For several the -us becomes -ī: *fluviī*, rivers. Read the tail, not the length of the word: *fluviī* is a plural even though it is barely longer than the singular.

teach.title: um-nouns: -um for one, -a for several
teach.say: *Oppidum* (town) ends in -um for one and -a for several: *oppida*, towns. Mark that plural -a now. It is the ending that catches beginners out, because it looks exactly like the -a of a single a-noun.

teach.title: The word after *est* or *sunt* names the subject too
teach.say: In *Brundisium et Tūsculum oppida Rōmāna sunt*, *oppida* is not on the receiving end of anything: it says what the subject is. A word that renames the subject after *est* (is) or *sunt* (are) wears the same naming form as the subject, so both halves of an ‘A is B’ sentence match.

teach.title: -a: one feminine thing, or several neuter ones
teach.say: *Īnsula* ends in -a and is one island. *Oppida* ends in -a and is several towns. Two different endings that look alike. The verb settles it — *est* for one, *sunt* for several — and so does the noun itself: an a-noun in -a is one, an um-noun in -a is many. There is a third -a besides: after *in* an a-noun lengthens to -ā (*in Italīā*, *in prōvinciā*), which is neither of those two and comes later, with the cases.

more.text: The learner's notes sort nouns by their first form: a-nouns (*ūva*, grape), us-nouns (*caseus*, cheese) and um-nouns (*pōculum*, cup); nouns in -r or -er (*vir*, man; *culter*, knife; *puer*, boy) count as us-nouns with a missing -us. Some change their stem before any ending is added (*culter, cultr-ī*; *carō, carn-is*), which is why a second form is learned with the word.

Plurals: -a becomes -ae, -us becomes -ī, -um becomes -a. That neuter plural -a looks like a feminine singular: *oppida* is 'towns', never 'a town'. Nouns of the other declensions (*pānis*, *pānēs*) follow later.

After *est* / *sunt* the word that describes or renames the subject is also nominative (*Nīlus fluvius est*; *Sicilia īnsula magna est*): both halves of an 'A is B' sentence wear the same ending. Ørberg's cap. I sets out singulāris / plūrālis; A&G §339 gives the nominative as the case of the subject and §283 the predicate nominative.
